questions.problem:
Given that 

$$
{∮}_{C}(x+y)\,dx-{x}^{2}y\,dy={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{5}\boxed{}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=25$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?
questions.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that 

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14152741/assets/0470588a034222b183694b087d417e8ead0d2fd72357e796373794d00523708f.png)

Since $P(x,y)=x+y$ and $Q(x,y)=-{x}^{2}y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(x+y)\,dx-{x}^{2}y\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-2xy-1)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 5,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(-2xy-1)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(-2\cdot r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}(-2{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r)\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{5}-{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral 

$$
{∮}_{C}({y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{cos}^{2}⁡x))\,dx+({x}^{2}+3xy)\,dy\,?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14152741/assets/4822bfa926feccb0a12c14580ac325f4f10a0e4f815d0247b2231bf08b8c2326.png)

Since $P(x,y)={y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{cos}^{2}⁡x)$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}+3xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2x+3y.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{cos}^{2}⁡x))\,dx+({x}^{2}+3xy)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+3y-2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2x+y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Given that $F(x,y)=⟨y+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+10)+2x⟩,$ which of the following is equivalent to ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr\,?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}(y+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3})\,dx+(\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+10)+2x)\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14152741/assets/93a1c20377ddd0731c6190712d9d6d77551124fa33001334e84f52049bb6b800.png)

Since $P(x,y)=y+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+10)+2x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1+2{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(y+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3})\,dx+(\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+10)+2x)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2-(1+2{y}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 9,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(1-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(1-2\cdot {r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\,{\int }_{0}^{9}(1-2{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )r\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14152741/assets/1f56006dd06fab3bbc736c45ac6e9d65a401b88e0a9eb8a5db404fb67b89977e.png)

Evaluate ${∮}_{C}({e}^{x}-8{x}^{2}y)dx+({y}^{7}+8x{y}^{2})\,dy,$ where the path $C$ is shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14152741/assets/f393d0facc98fe365e2c622e24223d6045b48b490937ba6e2f25d86d7eb4810f.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)={e}^{x}-8{x}^{2}y,\,Q(x,y)={y}^{7}+8x{y}^{2},
$$

 we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-8{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=8{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{x}-8{x}^{2}y)dx+({y}^{7}+8x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(8{y}^{2}-(-8{x}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}8({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 0\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}8({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}8({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2}8{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2}8{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}[2{r}^{4}]_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}32\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =32[\theta ]_{-\pi /2}^{0} \\  & =32\cdot \frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =16\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate ${∮}_{C}({x}^{2}-x{y}^{2})dx+(\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y)\,dy,$ where the path $C$ is shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14152741/assets/d816d9153e22dd109e20e3e387f6a0028e3f6a9eaf1d284dfae8b5fdf54cfc6e.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)={x}^{2}-x{y}^{2},\,Q(x,y)=\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y,
$$

 we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(\sqrt{x}-x{y}^{2})dx+(\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy-(-2xy))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4xy\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}4(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}2{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){\int }_{0}^{2}2{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){[\frac{{r}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )]_{0}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =4[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡0] \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$
